name: Koyukon
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Koyukon is not in the catalog. Both title-hit items were obtained and read: Thompson 1988 (ANLA handout, already on file; all 7 pages re-read as images) posits disjunct/conjunct/stem feet with left-headed s-w labelling to derive syncope, expansion and absorption, but contains no statement of stress placement; Leer 1976b (fetched sources this sweep from ANLA, https://uafanlc.alaska.edu/Online/CA965L1976b/, scanned typescript pp. 2-35) is a comparative Proto-Athabaskan paper on spirantization and the genesis of tone from vowel constriction, mentions Koyukon only in a consonant-reflex chart, and is silent on word stress. Neither adds a stress statement. The best first-hand stress statement read is Kroul 1975 sec. 1.15 (pp. 29-32; on file, verified against page images): primary stress on the stem syllable (verbs penult/final, nouns stem unless schwa), with a pre-stem exception for the nə-/də-/lə- thematic and tə- inceptive prefixes, secondary stress two syllables before primary, and some minimal pairs by stress; Jette 1907 (Man 7:54-55, on file) independently states all roots are accented, hence verb-final accent. No catalog record exists to confirm or supersede; Kroul 1975 is the candidate deciding source if Koyukon is added. Files and citations logged in (addendum stamped 2026-09-17T15:07Z).alaska.edu needs curl -k; its TLS chain is incomplete).

new_statements.quote: 1.15 Word Level Stress. Though there are minimal pairs distinguished only by phonemic stress, in the majority of instances word level stress is determined by the morphological structure of the word, the number of syllables, syllabic shape and type of vowel. [...] 1.15.4 Polysyllabic Words. Primary stress falls on the stem syllable in verbals, either in penultimate or final position. [...] In nouns, primary stress falls on the stem syllable unless it contains a shwa, in which case primary stress falls on the first syllable in trisyllabic nouns. Nouns with more than three syllables are more or less overtly verbal constructions, and behave like verbs.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (Kroul 1975 Wisconsin dissertation, fetched sources openly from ANLA), scanned at lines 490-608, and I rendered PDF pp. 41 and 43 (printed pp. 29, 31) to images and read them directly. The quoted passage is on the page verbatim: p.29 '1.15 Word Level Stress.Though there are minimal pairs distinguished only by phonemic stress, in the majority of instances word level stress is determined by the morphological structure of the word, the number of syllables, syllabic shape and type of vowel.' and p.31 'Polysyllabic Words. Primary stress falls on the stem syllable in verbals, either in penultimate or final position.... In nouns, primary stress falls on the stem syllable unless it co…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is largely predictable and stem-based: in polysyllabic words primary stress falls on the stem syllable (word-final, or penultimate when a suffix/enclitic follows); in nouns the stem is stressed unless its vowel is schwa (then the first syllable in trisyllables). Bisyllables are decided by word class and vowel quality (verbs and schwa+full-vowel words stress the final syllable; full+reduced and full+full stress the first; schwa+schwa stress the first if vowel-final, the last if consonant-final). Monosyllables are stressed. A few minimal pairs by stress exist.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of trisyllables whose primary stress is final; in longer words it falls two syllables before the primary-stressed syllable; at most one secondary stress per word; all other syllables unstressed (p.31). Jetté 1907 p.55 independently: extra accents on long syllables besides the root-accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs with thematic prefixes ne-, de-, le- (position 4) and inceptive-perfective/future forms with inceptive te- (position 5) take primary stress on the syllable BEFORE the stem (p.31); primary stress also falls on the possessive suffix -e' in kinship terms, negative -aa and interrogative -hee' after vowel-final stems, and prohibitive -yoo (p.32); some lexical minimal pairs distinguished only by stress (p.29).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in isolated words (nouns, verbs, particles) of the Central Outer (Central) dialect; author marks primary (acute) and secondary (grave) stress on citation forms. Corroborated by Jetté 1907 (Man 7, pp.54-55) for the Nulato-area dialects: 'All the roots are accented, and as these form the last syllable in verbs, it follows that all Ten'a verbs have an accent on the last syllable.'
new_statements.identity_note: Kroul 1975 describes 'Central Outer Koyukon' (villages Koyukuk, Galena, Ruby, Huslia; consultants Madeline Solomon and Doria Lolnitz) = the Central dialect of Koyukon in the Kari/Jones/Krauss (KAD 2000) terminology; Glottolog dialect code not verified. Jetté 1907 describes the 'central dialects' of Ten'a around Nulato (Lower and Central Koyukon of the Yukon). Neither describes Upper (Inner) Koyukon. Note the KAD intro (Krauss) reports low-marked tone surviving only in Lower Koyukon and the Toklat-Bearpaw subdialect of Upper; Kroul's Central Outer variety is treated as toneless with stress.

new_statements.quote: Primary stress falls on the stem syllable in verbals, either in penultimate or final position. The exception to this is in verbals with the thematic prefixes nə-, də- or lə- (position 4, see Section 2.4) or in inceptive perfective and future constructions with the inceptive prefix tə- (position 5, see Section 2.5), which take primary stress on the syllable before the stem. In nouns, primary stress falls on the stem syllable unless it contains a shwa, in which case primary stress falls on the first syllable in trisyllabic nouns. ... In greater-than-trisyllabic words, secondary stress falls two syllables before the syllable with primary stress.
new_statements.citation: Kroul, Mary Valentine (1975). The Phonology and Morphology of the Central Outer Koyukon Athapaskan Language. PhD dissertation, University of Wisconsin-Madison. xi+239 pp. ANLA KO973Kr1975a.
new_statements.locator: sec. 1.15 'Word Level Stress', pp. 29-32 (PDF pp. 41-44); quote from sec. 1.15.3 'Polysyllabic Words', p. 31 (PDF p. 43)
new_statements.reading: Morphologically governed stress: primary stress on the stem syllable (verbs: penult or final, since the stem is word-final or followed by one suffix; a few prefix classes pull stress to the pre-stem syllable); nouns likewise stem-stressed unless the stem vowel is schwa, then initial in trisyllables. Bisyllables (p. 29-30): verbs and schwa+full-vowel words final, full+reduced or full+full initial. Monosyllables stressed. Secondary stress two syllables before primary (initial in trisyllables with final primary). Kroul also notes minimal pairs 'distinguished only by phonemic stress' (p. 29). Jette 1907 (Man 7:54-55) agrees independently: all roots accented, so verbs accent the last syllable, with extra accents on long syllables. Fixed/morphological (stem-final-anchored) rather than a weight-driven or edge-counting system.

sources.citation: Leer, Jeff (1976). Spirantization and the Development of Suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan. Ms. dated 7-21-76, 24 pp. ms. + 30 pp. typescript (86-page scan). ANLA CA965L1976b.
sources.quote: One of the major purposes of this paper is to formulate a hypothesis of the development of tone in modern Athabaskan from an earlier (pre-Proto-Athabaskan) system of vowel nuclei. ... In PA there were two vocalic suprasegmentals, which in stems were restricted to closed syllables, and could co-occur. They are vowel nasalization and what I call vowel constriction. Vowel constriction is manifest in modern Athabaskan languages as tone. However, in PA it does not seem likely that this was tone as such
sources.locator: typescript p. 2 (PDF p. 3) and typescript sec. on PA suprasegmentals (PDF p. 13); Koyukon only in the consonant-reflex chart (PDF p. 23) and a suffix note (PDF p. 22)
sources.note: Comparative-historical study of Proto-Athabaskan closed-stem syllables, spirantization, and the origin of Athabaskan tone from PA vowel constriction (with Tlingit/Eyak parallels). The 'suprasegmentals' are PA tone/constriction and nasalization, not stress. Koyukon appears only as a row in the stem-final consonant reflex chart and in a remark that some Koyukon drops suffixed schwa after voiced finals. Nothing on Koyukon word stress or accent placement.

sources.citation: Jetté, Jules. 1907. On the Language of the Ten'a. Man 7, No. 36, pp. 51ff. (ANLA KO898J1907a)
sources.note: Sec. I.3 'Prosody and Accent' pp. 54-55: vowels have marked quantity; 'a distinct accent, marked, as in English, by a peculiar stress on the accented syllable'; 'All the roots are accented, and as these form the last syllable in verbs, it follows that all Ten'a verbs have an accent on the last syllable', exception disyllabic roots accented on their first syllable (penult); longer words carry extra (secondary) accents on long syllables; an emphatic 'drawl' (lengthening + higher pitch) falls only on accented syllables.
